```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(hypergraphs)
```

A mixed-membership topic model represents each topic as a distribution
over words and each document as a weighted combination of topics. This
allows an abstract about online teaching in medical education to receive
weight on more than one topic. The estimated weights describe the fitted
model's representation of the text; they are not externally validated
measurements of a document's true subjects.

This tutorial fits a topic model to COVID-19 education abstracts using
nonnegative matrix factorisation with Kullback–Leibler divergence. It
examines topic-count selection, variation across random starts, document
mixtures, and combinations of topics. A final comparison distinguishes
word-based topic mixtures from spectral clusters and their geometric
membership weights.

## The corpus

`covid_sample` contains 1,000 sampled abstracts about COVID-19 and
education published between 2020 and 2024. `clean_text()` removes selected
bibliographic markup and non-content strings. The stop list combines
`stop_words_en()` with corpus-defining terms chosen for removal. These
choices determine the vocabulary on which the model is estimated.

```{r corpus}
abstracts <- clean_text(covid_sample, column = "abstract")
boilerplate <- c("covid", "coronavirus", "sars", "cov", "pandemic",
                 "disease", "study", "studies", "result", "results",
                 "conclusion", "conclusions", "background", "method",
                 "methods", "objective", "aim")
stops <- c(stop_words_en(), boilerplate)
```

## The hypergraph

Construct a document–word hypergraph with abstracts as nodes, retained
words as hyperedges, and word counts as incidence weights. A word must
occur at least five times in the corpus to be retained. The example uses
dense storage so the same representation can be reused in the later
clustering examples. Storage type does not define the topic model.

```{r hypergraph}
abstracts_hg <- text_hypergraph(abstracts, column = "abstract", id = "doc",
                                stop_words = stops, min_count = 5,
                                min_chars = 2, sparse = FALSE)
abstracts_hg
```

```{r hypergraph-values, include = FALSE}
vocabulary <- hg_get(abstracts_hg, what = "vocabulary")
```

The resulting matrix contains `r abstracts_hg$n_nodes` abstract rows
and `r format(nrow(vocabulary), big.mark = ",")` word columns. These are
the document and vocabulary units used in the following fits.

## How many topics

The number of topics is a model specification. Compare candidate
values using both numerical diagnostics and document interpretation.
Semantic coherence evaluates co-occurrence among a topic's highest-ranked
words (Mimno et al. 2011). The implemented UMass score adds 0.01 to both
the joint document count and the document count of the earlier-ranked
word, then sums the logarithms of their ratios. This follows the smoothing
convention used by `stm`. Scores nearer zero indicate stronger
co-occurrence; the score cannot be positive.

FREX combines frequency and exclusivity ranks through a weighted harmonic
mean, summarised over the top words (Bischof and Airoldi 2012). It favours
terms that are frequent within a topic and relatively concentrated there.
A candidate is on the plotted frontier when no other candidate has larger
values on both diagnostics. Frontier membership narrows the comparison
but does not select a uniquely correct topic count.

`hg_topic_search()` fits models with 4, 8, 12, 16, and 20 topics, using
two random starts per candidate. It reports mean coherence and mean
exclusivity over the ten most probable words of each topic. More starts
would provide a more informative assessment of optimisation variability.

```{r topic-search}
topic_search <- hg_topic_search(abstracts_hg, k = seq(4, 20, by = 4),
                                nstart = 2, parallel = TRUE, n_cores = 2)
topic_search
```

```{r topic-search-plot}
plot(topic_search)
```

```{r topic-search-values, include = FALSE}
k4 <- subset(topic_search, k == 4)
k16 <- subset(topic_search, k == 16)
k20 <- subset(topic_search, k == 20)
on_frontier <- subset(topic_search, frontier)
frontier_k <- sub(", ([^,]*)$", " and \\1", toString(on_frontier$k))
```

Mean coherence is `r round(k4$coherence, 1)` for four topics,
`r round(k16$coherence, 1)` for 16, and `r round(k20$coherence, 1)` for 20.
The corresponding exclusivity values are `r round(k4$exclusivity, 2)`,
`r round(k16$exclusivity, 2)`, and `r round(k20$exclusivity, 2)`.
Models with `r frontier_k` topics are on the diagnostic frontier.
The detailed example uses 16 topics to match the number used by Saqr
et al. (2023). This is an analytical choice for comparison, rather than
a conclusion established by the two diagnostics.

## A mixed-membership model of 16 topics

`hg_topics()` approximates the document–word count matrix by the
product of a document–topic factor and a topic–word factor. Both factors
are nonnegative. The multiplicative updates of Lee and Seung (2001)
minimise generalised Kullback–Leibler divergence. This objective is related
to the likelihood of probabilistic latent semantic analysis (Hofmann 1999;
Gaussier and Goutte 2005); the numerical optimisation can reach a local
solution.

To obtain topic word probabilities, normalise each topic's word weights.
To obtain document topic shares, first multiply the document–topic weights
by each topic's total word mass, then normalise within documents. This
adjustment makes the shares invariant to reciprocal rescaling of the
two factors. Each document's topic shares sum to one.

Fit the model from five random starts and retain the fit with the
smallest divergence. To compare starts, topics are matched one-to-one by
the Hungarian algorithm using agreement between their ranked word lists.
The agreement score averages Jaccard similarity at depths one through ten
(Greene et al. 2014). A high score indicates reproducibility of the top-word
description across these starts; it does not measure accuracy against
known topics.

```{r topic-model}
topic_model <- hg_topics(abstracts_hg, k = 16, nstart = 5, parallel = TRUE,
                         n_cores = 2)
topic_model
```

```{r topic-model-values, include = FALSE}
topic_table <- hg_get(topic_model)
largest <- subset(topic_table, prevalence == max(prevalence))
smallest <- subset(topic_table, prevalence == min(prevalence))
```

Prevalence is the mean topic share across documents. The `documents`
column sums those shares and can be read as a fractional document count.
It is not the number of abstracts exclusively assigned to the topic.
The most prevalent topic, described by `r largest$top_words`, has mean
share `r round(100 * largest$prevalence, 1)`%; the least prevalent,
described by `r smallest$top_words`, has mean share
`r round(100 * smallest$prevalence, 1)`%.
Mean agreement across topics is `r round(mean(topic_table$agreement), 2)`.
Low agreement warrants inspection of the alternative fits and their
convergence, rather than a substantive interpretation of one run alone.

```{r topic-model-plot, fig.height = 9}
plot(topic_model)
```

## How mixed the abstracts are

For a compact document summary, identify the topic with the largest
estimated share. This dominant-topic label retains only one part of the
document's mixture.

```{r main-topics}
main_topics <- hg_get(topic_model, what = "documents")
head(main_topics)
```

```{r main-topic-values, include = FALSE}
main_share <- main_topics$share
share_quartiles <- quantile(main_share, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
```

The median dominant-topic share is `r round(share_quartiles[2], 2)`,
with an interquartile range from `r round(share_quartiles[1], 2)` to
`r round(share_quartiles[3], 2)`.
Dominant shares reach at least 0.9 in
`r round(100 * mean(main_share >= 0.9), 1)`% of abstracts, while
`r round(100 * mean(main_share < 0.5), 1)`% have no share exceeding 0.5.
These summaries quantify concentration under this fitted model.

Inspect a document with substantial weight on more than one topic.
The following example selects the abstract with the largest second-ranked
topic share and displays its text alongside the shares of at least 0.05.

```{r example-choice, include = FALSE}
shares <- hg_get(topic_model, what = "shares")
second_share <- tapply(shares$share, shares$node,
                       \(s) sort(s, decreasing = TRUE)[2])
example_id <- names(which.max(second_share))
```

```{r example-shares}
example_shares <- subset(shares, node == example_id & share >= 0.05)
example_shares
```

```{r example-text}
example_abstract <- subset(abstracts, doc == example_id)
with(example_abstract, writeLines(strwrap(abstract, 78)))
```

```{r example-values, include = FALSE}
ranked <- example_shares[order(-example_shares$share), ]
words_of <- function(label) subset(topic_table, topic == label)$top_words
```

This abstract assigns share `r round(ranked$share[1], 2)` to the topic
described by `r words_of(ranked$topic[1])` and
`r round(ranked$share[2], 2)` to the topic described by
`r words_of(ranked$topic[2])`. Reading the abstract permits a substantive
check of both descriptions. A dominant-topic label would omit the second
share from the summary.

## Topic quality

Evaluate each fitted topic using the same coherence and exclusivity
definitions used in the candidate comparison. The reported topic size is
its fractional document count. These diagnostics can identify topics for
closer inspection, but they do not replace reading the underlying text.

```{r model-quality}
model_quality <- hg_topic_quality(abstracts_hg, topics = topic_model)
model_quality
```

```{r model-quality-plot}
plot(model_quality)
```

## Topic combinations

Topic combinations provide another summary of document mixtures.
First define which topics are considered present in each document.
Each resulting set can be represented as a hyperedge, with topics as nodes.
Identical combinations are counted across documents. This retains the
complete selected set, whereas a pairwise network retains only its pairs.

The example treats a topic as present when its share is at least 0.2.
This threshold is more than three times the equal share of 1/16 and is
an explicit reporting choice. `min_size = 2` selects documents containing
at least two topics above that threshold; `top = Inf` retains every
observed combination. Related threshold-based topic networks are used by
Abuhay et al. (2017) and Cassi et al. (2017).

```{r topic-sets}
topic_sets <- group_hypergraph(topic_model, threshold = 0.2, min_size = 2,
                               top = Inf)
combinations <- hg_get(topic_sets, what = "sets")
head(combinations)
```

```{r topic-sets-values, include = FALSE}
multi_share <- function(threshold) {
  sets <- hg_get(group_hypergraph(topic_model, threshold = threshold,
                                  min_size = 2, top = Inf), what = "sets")
  sum(sets$count) / abstracts_hg$n_nodes
}
n_combining <- sum(combinations$count)
```

At threshold 0.2,
`r round(100 * n_combining / abstracts_hg$n_nodes, 1)`% of abstracts have
at least two selected topics, forming `r nrow(combinations)` distinct
combinations. This proportion changes to
`r round(100 * multi_share(0.1), 1)`% at threshold 0.1 and
`r round(100 * multi_share(0.3), 1)`% at threshold 0.3.
Report the threshold with the resulting counts.

The plot displays the eight most frequent combinations containing at
least three selected topics. Regions enclose topic sets, colour indicates
the number of abstracts with that set, and node size summarises
participation in the displayed combinations.

```{r topic-sets-plot, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 7}
frequent_triples <- group_hypergraph(topic_model, threshold = 0.2,
                                     min_size = 3, top = 8)
plot(frequent_triples, group = "All documents")
```

Use `group` to count combinations separately by a document attribute.
The following example reports the two most frequent combinations within
each publication year.

```{r topic-sets-year}
sets_by_year <- group_hypergraph(topic_model, threshold = 0.2, min_size = 2,
                                 group = "year", top = 2)
hg_get(sets_by_year, what = "sets")
```

## The network of topics

With the same presence threshold, `topic_network()` connects two
topics with a weight equal to the number of abstracts in which both are
selected. The plot retains weights at or above their upper quartile.
This graph summarises pairwise co-occurrence, while the preceding
hypergraph retains combinations of three or more topics as units.

```{r topic-network}
topic_pairs <- topic_network(abstracts_hg, topics = topic_model,
                             threshold = 0.2)
strong_pair <- with(topic_pairs, quantile(weight, 0.75))
network_view <- topic_network(abstracts_hg, topics = topic_model,
                                 threshold = 0.2, what = "network")
cograph::splot(network_view, minimum = strong_pair,
               edge_width_range = c(0.5, 6), node_fill = "#56B4E9",
               edge_color = "#0072B2")
```

Without a threshold, `topic_network()` instead calculates correlations
between document topic shares, following the simple topic-correlation
approach described by Roberts et al. (2019). Correlation and thresholded
co-occurrence are different definitions of a topic relation and should
not be interpreted interchangeably.

## A partition of the abstracts

A hard partition assigns exactly one cluster to each abstract. This
can be useful for group comparisons even when documents have mixed
content, provided that the loss of graded membership is explicit.
For comparison, `hg_cluster()` uses eigenvectors associated with the
16 smallest eigenvalues of the Zhou Laplacian and partitions the resulting
embedding by k-means. This clustering objective differs from the
word-reconstruction objective of the topic model.

```{r clusters}
clusters <- hg_cluster(abstracts_hg, k = 16, seed = 1)
cluster_quality <- hg_topic_quality(abstracts_hg, clusters = clusters)
cluster_quality
```

```{r cluster-agreement}
hg_agreement(clusters, main_topics, label = c("cluster", "topic"),
             method = c("ari", "nmi"))
```

```{r cluster-values, include = FALSE}
cluster_agreement <- hg_agreement(clusters, main_topics,
                                  label = c("cluster", "topic"),
                                  method = c("ari", "nmi"))
```

Mean coherence and exclusivity are
`r round(mean(cluster_quality$coherence), 1)` and
`r round(mean(cluster_quality$exclusivity), 2)` for the spectral clusters,
compared with `r round(mean(model_quality$coherence), 1)` and
`r round(mean(model_quality$exclusivity), 2)` for the topic model.
The adjusted Rand index between the cluster partition and the
dominant-topic partition is `r round(cluster_agreement$ari, 2)`.
This measures agreement between two hard summaries; it does not compare
the complete topic mixtures or establish which model is more valid.

Symmetric nonnegative matrix factorisation provides a different set
of graded memberships by approximating the document-similarity matrix
defined by the hypergraph Laplacian (Kuang et al. 2012; Hayashi et al. 2020).
The resulting nonnegative document weights are normalised across clusters.
They describe a factorisation of similarity rather than a generative
model of word counts, and should therefore be distinguished from the
topic shares estimated above.

```{r symnmf}
cluster_membership <- hg_cluster(abstracts_hg, k = 16, algorithm = "symnmf",
                                 seed = 1, nstart = 5, what = "membership")
subset(cluster_membership, node == "2-s2.0-85101300775" & membership >= 0.05)
```

```{r symnmf-values, include = FALSE}
cluster_main <- tapply(cluster_membership$membership,
                       cluster_membership$node, max)
```

For these similarity-based memberships, the median largest weight is
`r round(median(cluster_main), 2)`, and
`r round(100 * mean(cluster_main >= 0.9), 1)`% of documents have a largest
weight of at least 0.9. Compare these concentrations with the topic-model
shares while retaining the distinction between the two objectives and
their different membership interpretations.
